holding_summary: The Texas Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the state zoning enabling statute and the City of Dallas zoning ordinance excluding business, apartment, and other non-residential uses from single-family residential districts, as a valid exercise of the police power. In doing so the court reasoned at length that apartment and tenement houses have historically been treated as a class 'peculiarly subject to' police-power regulation because of associated overcrowding, disease, and crime concerns, and affirmed exclusion of a gasoline filling station from a residential district on that reasoning.

quotes.text: Apartment or Tenement Houses have always been regarded as peculiarly subject to the police power.

What we have determined here is that the zoning statutes are valid and that the ordinance before us in its general scope and dominant features, so far as its provisions are here involved, is a valid exercise of authority.

holding_summary: An oil-lease pumper was injured in a gas explosion inside a small lease house on his employer's property, which he occupied under an arrangement deducting $10 per month from his wages as rent. The Texas Supreme Court held that even assuming a landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties as to the house, that relationship is not inconsistent with the master-servant relationship, and because the pumper's occupancy of the house was necessarily incident to the round-the-clock and later twelve-hour duty required by his job, he remained an employee acting in the course of employment to whom common-law duties of care were owed.

quotes.text: there is no inconsistency between the relation of landlord and tenant and that of master and servant.
there is no inconsistency between the relation of landlord and tenant and that of master and servant.
The judgment of the Court of Civil Appeals affirming that of the trial court is affirmed.

Dispute between a mortgagee claiming possession rights and a landlord over rent owed for a commercial storefront occupancy; not a lodging or boarding arrangement.

holding_summary: Mrs. Abernathy purchased an apartment house, occupied one apartment herself with her husband and rented another to a tenant for $70 per month, paid taxes and interest, and later sold her equity. The Texas Supreme Court held that in doing so she merely exercised the ordinary incidents of ownership -- including the right to lease part of the property -- and committed no wrong that could estop her from later pleading coverture as a defense to personal liability on the purchase-money note.

quotes.text: Among those incidents were the right of possession and use, the right to lease, and the right to sell the property, subject, of course, to appellant’s lien.
Among those incidents were the right of possession and use, the right to lease, and the right to sell the property, subject, of course, to appellant’s lien.
By using one of the apartments, leasing another and selling her equity she was but doing that which she had a legal right to do.

holding_summary: Construing a 1940 subdivision restrictive-covenant instrument that barred hotels, rooming houses, boarding houses, and other business uses on any lot, but shall be used for residence purposes only -- with a proviso that renting out a single room was not itself a prohibited use, only operating a regular rooming or boarding house being barred -- the court held that because the covenant restricted only houses actually built on the lots (not the lots or 'buildings' generally) to residential use, it did not prevent the Y.M.C.A. from erecting and using a non-residential building for religious, educational, and physical-development purposes.

quotes.text: The mention of rooming house or boarding house does not prohibit the renting out of one room, but is intended only to prevent the running of a regular rooming or boarding house.
We hold that they do not.

holding_summary: Construing a 1919 trust agreement and conveyance creating the exclusive Shadyside residential subdivision in Houston, the Texas Supreme Court held that the instrument's building and use restrictions -- including a clause permanently barring any business house, saloon, hospital, public boarding house, place of public entertainment, store, livery stable, or other place of business or public resort from ever being erected on the lots -- were of perpetual or indefinite duration and did not automatically expire with the twenty-one-year administrative trust term.

quotes.text: No business house or houses, saloon, hospital, public boarding house, place of public entertainment, store, livery stable, or other place of business or public resort, shall ever be erected on any part of said land, nor shall any telegraph, telephone or electric light poles or overhead structures ever be erected on any part of said property except on a space five feet in width along the West line of the larger tract.
We conclude that the building and use restrictions imposed by the written instrument in question on the lots in Shadyside will not expire on June 30th, but are of permanent and indefinite duration.

notes: characterization left null: the 'public boarding house' prohibition appears as quoted covenant text whose duration is the issue decided; the case does not adjudicate a specific letting arrangement.

holding_summary: Applying a subdivision restrictive covenant limiting lots to residence purposes only -- with a proviso that the prohibition on operating a rooming house or boarding house did not prohibit renting one room, but was intended only to prevent running a regular rooming or boarding house -- the court of civil appeals held that the Episcopal Church's use of a house near a university campus for weekly communion services, student discussion meetings, and a daily open house for students was a distinct and substantial breach of the residential-only restriction, and enjoined the use despite evidence of surrounding neighborhood change.

The use of the property by appellant in the instant case constitutes a distinct and substantial breach of the restrictive covenant and the trial court did not err in granting injunctive relief.

holding_summary: Applying a mutual restrictive-covenant agreement among subdivision lot owners limiting use to residential purposes only -- with the mention of rooming house or boarding house intended only to prevent running a regular rooming or boarding house, not to bar renting out one room -- the court of civil appeals held that a local college fraternity's lease and use of a residence as a chapter house, with vending-machine food and beverage sales, meetings, initiations, and social gatherings, violated the restriction, and enjoined the fraternity-house use.
